title: Shortness of breath in a 68-year-old (ED)

patient.name: Harold Bennett
patient.chiefComplaint: Worsening shortness of breath for two weeks
patient.setting: Emergency department, sitting upright on a stretcher

persona.affect: Tired, a little breathless, polite, worried but trying to make light of it
persona.speakingStyle: Short sentences; pauses to catch his breath after longer answers; plain everyday words, no medical jargon
persona.worries: Worried he will be admitted and miss his granddaughter’s birthday this weekend; quietly worried it is his heart again
persona.background: Retired city bus driver, married, enjoys fishing and his grandchildren

doorSign.task: Mr. Bennett, 68, presents with two weeks of worsening shortness of breath. Take a focused history, perform a focused cardiovascular and respiratory examination, then present your summary, differential diagnosis and initial plan.

doorInstructions.task: Take a focused history and perform a focused physical examination. Share your impressions with the patient before you leave. You will then write a post-encounter note.

history.openingStatement: I just can’t catch my breath. It’s been getting worse for a couple of weeks.

facts.answer: It came on gradually about two weeks ago and has got steadily worse. The last three days have been the worst.
Two weeks ago I could walk a few blocks. Now I get winded walking from the bedroom to the kitchen, or going up the 12 stairs at home.
I can’t lie flat any more. I’ve been sleeping on three pillows, and last night I slept in my recliner.
Yes, a couple of times this week I woke up gasping and had to sit on the edge of the bed for a few minutes.
My ankles have been puffy for about a week, worse by the evening. My shoes are tight.
I’ve put on about 4 kilos — nine pounds — in the last two weeks, even though I’m not eating much.
A dry tickly cough, mostly at night when I lie down. Nothing coming up.
My belly feels full and a bit sore on the right side, and I’ve not had much appetite.
I’m wiped out all the time.
I’m up two or three times a night to pass water.
I ran out of my water pill about ten days ago and didn’t get it refilled — I hate being stuck near a bathroom when I’m out.
We had a lot of family over for my wife’s 70th — lots of takeout, ham, chips. More salt than I’m supposed to have.
I had a heart attack in 2019 — they put a stent in. Since then they’ve said my heart pumps weakly. I also have high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes and high cholesterol.

facts.topic: What he was told about his heart
facts.answer: The heart doctor said it pumps at about 30 percent. I had a scan last spring.
The stent in 2019 through my wrist, and my appendix out when I was 20.

Furosemide 40 mg in the morning — the one I ran out of. Carvedilol 12.5 mg twice a day, lisinopril 10 mg once a day, spironolactone 25 mg, aspirin 81 mg, atorvastatin 80 mg at night, and metformin 1000 mg twice a day. No over-the-counter stuff except some ibuprofen for my knee last week.
Penicillin gave me a rash all over as a kid. No food allergies.
My dad died of a heart attack at 62. My mom had a stroke and died at 80. I have one brother, he’s 71 and has diabetes.
I smoked a pack a day for 30 years and quit after the heart attack in 2019.
A beer or two on the weekend. Not more.
No, never.
Retired. I drove city buses for 35 years.
With my wife, Carol. Our daughter lives ten minutes away.
My grandkids, and fishing at the lake with my brother.
Married forty-five years, just my wife. Not much going on lately with how tired I’ve been.
No trips. Haven’t been further than the grocery store in a month.
I’m scared it’s my heart again. And I really want to be home for my granddaughter’s birthday on Saturday.

pertinentNegatives.answer: No chest pain or pressure. Not like the heart attack.
Nothing coming up, and no blood.
No racing heart that I’ve noticed, and I haven’t passed out.
No, both legs are the same. No pain in my calves.
No colds, nobody sick at home.
No weakness, numbness or trouble speaking.

pertinentNegatives.topic: Urinary symptoms other than frequency at night
pertinentNegatives.answer: No burning or blood in the urine.
I’m a bit fed up, but not depressed.

unknownPolicy.unknownReply: Hmm, I’m not sure. I haven’t noticed anything like that.

general_appearance.default: Older man sitting bolt upright, mildly breathless at rest, pausing mid-sentence to breathe; alert and oriented; looks tired.

pulse_radial.default: Radial pulse {vitals.hr} beats/min, regular rhythm, low volume.

jvp_inspection.default: JVP clearly elevated: venous column about 9 cm above the sternal angle at 30° (estimated RAP ~14 cmH2O), pulsating up to the angle of the jaw.

hepatojugular_reflux.default: Positive: with sustained right upper quadrant pressure the JVP rises about 4 cm and stays up while pressure is held.

precordial_inspection.default: Apical impulse visible lateral to the midclavicular line; no scars or deformity.

pmi_palpation.cardiac_mitral: PMI displaced laterally to the 6th intercostal space at the anterior axillary line; diffuse (about 4 cm).

cardiac_mitral.text: Tachycardic, regular. Soft grade 2/6 holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating toward the axilla. A low-pitched extra sound after S2 is faintly audible.

default.text: Tachycardic, regular rhythm; normal S1 and S2; no murmur at this area.

cardiac_mitral.text: Low-pitched S3 gallop at the apex, loudest with the patient rolled onto the left side.

left_lateral_decubitus.text: Loud low-pitched S3 gallop at the apex — clearest with the patient rolled onto the left side.

cardiac_tricuspid.text: Faint low-pitched extra sound after S2, better heard at the apex.

peripheral_pulses.foot_right: Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses 1+, hard to feel through the edema.
peripheral_pulses.foot_left: Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses 1+, hard to feel through the edema.

edema_assessment.ankle_left: 3+ pitting edema; deep impression persists after pressure.
edema_assessment.foot_right: Pitting edema over the dorsum of the foot.
edema_assessment.foot_left: Pitting edema over the dorsum of the foot.

chest_inspection.default: Mildly increased work of breathing with visible neck accessory muscle use; symmetric expansion; no scars.

lung_post_ll.text: Fine end-inspiratory crackles over the lower third of the lung field.

lung_lat_r.text: Fine crackles at the lateral base.

lung_lat_l.text: Fine crackles at the lateral base.

lung_ant_rl.text: Scattered fine crackles at end inspiration.

lung_ant_ll.text: Scattered fine crackles at end inspiration.

chest_percussion.lung_post_rl: Dull to percussion over the lowest part of the right base.
chest_percussion.lung_post_ll: Slightly dull at the left base.
chest_percussion.lung_lat_r: Dull at the right lateral base.

tactile_fremitus.lung_post_rl: Tactile fremitus reduced at the right base.

vocal_resonance.lung_post_rl: Vocal resonance reduced at the right base; no egophony.

abd_inspection.default: Mildly distended; no visible veins or bruising.
abd_inspection.abd_rlq: Small, well-healed oblique scar in the right lower quadrant.

abd_light_palpation.abd_ruq: Mild tenderness in the right upper quadrant without guarding.

liver_palpation.abd_ruq: Smooth, mildly tender liver edge palpable about 3 cm below the right costal margin.

skin_inspection.shin_right: Shiny, taut skin over the swollen shin; no ulcers or erythema.
skin_inspection.shin_left: Shiny, taut skin over the swollen shin; no ulcers or erythema.

expectedDifferential.diagnosis: Acute decompensated heart failure (HFrEF, ischaemic cardiomyopathy)
expectedDifferential.rationale: Known EF ~30% after MI; orthopnea, PND, weight gain, bilateral pitting edema, raised JVP, positive HJR, displaced PMI, S3, bibasal crackles and right effusion. Precipitants: stopped furosemide, dietary salt load, recent NSAID.

expectedDifferential.diagnosis: Acute coronary syndrome as a precipitant
expectedDifferential.rationale: Prior MI and multiple risk factors; must be excluded with ECG and troponin even without chest pain (silent ischaemia in diabetes).
Crackles and hypoxia, but afebrile, dry cough and bilateral findings with edema argue against.
Tachycardia and hypoxia; less likely given symmetric edema, gradual course and clear volume overload.
30 pack-year history, but no wheeze or sputum and clear signs of fluid overload.

expectedDifferential.diagnosis: Other causes of fluid overload (renal failure, cirrhosis)
expectedDifferential.rationale: Consider with labs; cardiac signs make these less likely.
